extracted.intended_audience: federal agency regulatory analysts, rulewriters, and OIRA reviewers preparing or evaluating regulatory impact analyses (RIAs)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting and presenting regulatory benefit-cost analyses for U.S. federal regulations, covering scope (spatial and temporal), analytic baselines, discounting, and treatment of international effects. Intended to inform agencies how to prepare analyses that support policymaking and transparent public disclosure under Executive Order 12866 and related authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing the benefits and costs of regulatory alternatives helps policymakers arrive at sound regulatory decisions and helps the public and other branches of government understand the effects of those decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful analysis can facilitate the development of well-designed regulations and thereby increase net benefits for society as a whole. Agencies should perform benefit-cost analysis to inform decisionmaking and public understanding. (Intro)

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial scope of analysis — primary focus and consideration of noncitizens abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary analyses of regulations can often continue to focus on effects experienced by citizens and residents of the United States, but U.S. citizens and residents are frequently affected indirectly through effects on noncitizens residing abroad, and such effects may be important for analysts to estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include effects on noncitizens residing abroad when: assessing them provides a useful proxy for effects on U.S. citizens/residents that are difficult to estimate; they proxy U.S. national interests not otherwise captured (e.g., national security, diplomatic interests); regulating an externality on the basis of global effects supports international cooperation; or international/domestic legal obligations require or support a global calculation. Explain choices about geographic scope and maintain consistency across categories of benefits/costs, or justify why scope varies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency in geographic scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize the importance of consistency in the scope of analysis used to analyze benefits and costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid analyses that account for certain benefits/costs accruing to noncitizens abroad while omitting others without adequate explanation. Where scope varies across categories, explain why the scope differs and the implications for results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of international reciprocity and iterated actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciprocity-related evidence (e.g., likely responses by foreign governments such as tit-for-tat actions) must be examined on a context-specific basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether reciprocity or free-riding is likely in the particular context. Do not assume reciprocity universally; use the same standards of evidence and estimation for likely foreign government policies as for state or other governments. Predictions should be supported with evidence; consider legal and practical limits to including such effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary versus supplementary analysis for global effects
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no one-size-fits-all rule that global-effects analyses must always be primary or always be supplementary; context determines whether including effects on noncitizens abroad in a primary analysis is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases where global-effects estimates are de minimis or costly to produce, supplementary analysis may suffice. Agencies should decide based on evidence, cost-benefit of producing estimates, and potential to mislead if separated. If the primary analysis focuses on global effects, consider producing a separate supplementary analysis of effects experienced by U.S. citizens/residents unless separation is impractical or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The temporal scope of analyses should be long enough to encompass all of the important effects that are likely to result from the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an analytical timeframe that captures effects relevant to the public and policymakers; consider whether the choice of ending point could change the sign of net benefits or the ranking of alternatives. Agencies should examine sensitivity to analytical timeframe where appropriate and should not set arbitrary limits on projecting into the future when evidence supports longer horizons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic baselines are forecasts (no-action baseline)
rubrics_metrics.description: An appropriate standard (i.e., no-action) baseline is not a description of the status quo; it is a forecast of the way the world would look absent the regulatory action being assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baselines should be grounded in sound theoretical and empirical evidence about current conditions and ongoing and anticipated future trends. Do not default to 'status quo' without evidence. Use best available forecasts; document assumptions and evidence supporting baseline forecasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of expected government actions into the baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: The baseline should attempt to reflect relevant final rules and proposed rules or other previously announced policy changes that the agency is reasonably certain will be finalized before the rule under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects of regulatory and other policy changes induced by the regulation under consideration should generally be attributed to the future actions themselves (not to the baseline of the current rule). Agencies are encouraged to consider likely paths of future government programs and policies either in the primary baseline or in a supplemental baseline, and to carefully describe how those future policies affect the analysis. Predictions must be supported with reasonable evidence; where induced future policies are a consequence of the action under review, attribute effects to those future actions and not to the baseline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-statutory (without-statute) vs post-statutory (with-statute) baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, an agency’s first regulatory action implementing a new statutory authority should be assessed against a pre-statutory (without-statute) baseline; however, if substantial portions of a regulation simply restate statutory requirements that are self-implementing or over which the agency has little or no regulatory discretion, agencies may use a post-statutory (with-statute) baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use without-statute baselines to assess the effects of the statute itself when informative and feasible; use with-statute baselines to focus analysis on discretionary elements when the statute leaves little agency discretion. Explain choice and implications for interpretation of benefits/costs. Avoid confusing terminology; OMB supports clarifying terms to with-statute/without-statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of induced effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of future policies or regulatory actions that are induced by the regulation under consideration should generally be attributed to those future actions themselves, not folded into the baseline for the current action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not incorporate future policy changes that are responses to the current regulation into the baseline used to evaluate the current regulation; instead treat them as consequences of other future actions and attribute effects accordingly. Consult with OMB for particular cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discounting approach — descriptive default and updating
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB generally recommends a descriptive approach to discounting that reflects market and empirical evidence (e.g., Treasury and TIPS markets) for estimating the social rate of time preference (SRTP), while acknowledging prescriptive arguments for lower rates for very long horizons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB will provide a default SRTP and a long-term declining discount rate schedule (generated via a model such as Bauer-Rudebusch adapted by OMB) over a 150-year horizon; agencies may choose other approaches when appropriate. OMB will update the SRTP and long-term schedule every three years in an appendix to the Circular. Document choice of discounting approach and perform sensitivity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term discounting and declining discount rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncertainty about the appropriate value of the discount rate implies that the certainty-equivalent discount rate will decline over long horizons; OMB is considering (and adopts in final text) a default schedule that declines over time to capture this insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may apply the default declining schedule or an alternative supported by evidence. Be aware of modeling choices (e.g., non-negativity constraints) that affect the decline. Update declining schedules regularly to avoid time-inconsistency concerns and perform sensitivity analyses. Use model detail and justification when adopting long-term declining rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for risk when discounting (certainty-equivalent approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should calculate both a certainty-equivalent value of benefits and costs and a certainty-equivalent value of the discount rate when appropriate, because uncertainty in discount rates reduces the certainty-equivalent discount rate over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between uncertainty in discount rates and uncertainty in benefit/cost streams; apply the certainty-equivalent approach where appropriate and document assumptions. Note that applying a declining discount rate schedule is consistent with computing certainty-equivalent discount factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical considerations for intergenerational impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Special ethical considerations arise when comparing benefits and costs across generations; some believe it is ethically impermissible to discount the utility of future generations, which motivates prescriptive approaches to discounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular A-4 discusses prescriptive considerations but generally recommends descriptive approaches for default discounting; when ethical/prescriptive arguments are used (e.g., very low or zero rates for the far future), document justification and consider sensitivity analyses reflecting those prescriptive choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limitation of modeling approaches (e.g., Ramsey and model-based approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model-based approaches such as the Ramsey formula or models that endogenize the discount rate can be useful in specific circumstances, but OMB balances their potential virtues against the benefits of a descriptive default tied to market data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB has reduced emphasis on the Ramsey approach in the Circular but notes model-based approaches' potential utility. Agencies may employ such models where appropriate but should justify their use and compare results to descriptive default approaches; OMB will provide a default descriptive approach for broad applicability.
